And while that lack of gratitude still hangs like an irksome shadow over those many years, there are, much more prominently, the memories of having shared that final chapter with mom, of having made each day count for something, for having kept a promise, and most of all, in the midst of her decline, of having been able to make her smile, and laugh, and embrace each day to her last, without her feeling fear or regret. comments.body:
Don’t be fooled. Dario loves being rich and wants to be richer. He has a very clear plan to achieve that goal and he sticks to it.  In his speech at the NASDAQ just before the market opened Thursday, he clearly stated that he believes most of the money spent on AI will go to the best model, which will also be the most expensive model to use. And the best model also makes the best smaller and lower cost models.

That’s his plan. It’s clear. It’s logical. It’s the opposite of “weird.”

ANT investors this only have three questions to answer:
1) Is Dario right?
2) Does creating the best model require an AI lab singularly focused on that objective or will the ability to create great models proliferate and actually become easy for many people to do?
3) If only a few organizations can do it, is ANT the one most likely to be always or at least mostly in the lead?

Those questions are hard enough to answer. The rest of this PR about weirdness and altruism is just noise.

More importantly, machine intelligence can be implemented in a number of ways that differ significantly from today's technology - which is rathe complex and clumsy. It's simply the first generation of machine intelligence that has demonstrated itself as being useful. Think of it as the first generation of the iPhone. Along comes another technology in a couple of years and we have zillions of dollars worth of data centers sitting idle.

Today's version of AI appears to be "intelligent" but it simply cannot think outside the box in which it has been trained. In fact it doesn't "think" at all. Human beings will always have the advantage in this regard.

comments.name: Wendy B.
comments.body: Sourdough starter is just a culture of yeast and lactic acid bacteria. In microbiology labs, since maintaining a live culture is time-consuming and requires resources, live cultures are often stored in various ways, such as slants, frozen, and dehydrated. The yeast they sell for bread making is grown in a huge vat and then just dehydrated for sale in stores. No different than dehydrating sourdough starter (lactic acid bacteria don't have a good survival rate unless you freeze-dry, though; you can't just dry it in a warm oven or food dehydrator). In fact,many commercial bakeries have used dried sourdough starter for decades.

I can see from commenters recommendations that Hawaii, where I lived for many years, has its work cut out for it! 

Hawaiian sea salt is a hugely popular and (at least locally) hyped. It's available in  dramatic colors: pin, red, and black, along with austere white. No tourist venue is complete without it, fetchingly displayed in cute packaging. 

I see it as harmless pleasure, an affordable tourist souvenir that does not involve hiring children in Indonesia or the Philippines to manufacture it or factories in China to mass-produce it. In Hawaii, you don't have to be rich to enjoy local sea salt. And compared to so many tourist gifts it has a low environmental impact.

Personally, I prefer Sea Salt that is naturally evaporated from waters of the Tropical Atlantic. Hard to find but definitely "lighter" and "brighter" than stuff from the other parts of the globe.
In addition to the flavour, "Sea Salt" does what it does in many recipes due to the distinctively large flakes as opposed to the tiny grains of industrially produced salt. That doesnt change with the provenance of the salt.

comments.body: A cancer diagnosis has a way of immediately clarifying which people in your life truly have your back and who doesn't. It strips the masks off and reveals people's true character. Some of the people you think will be there for you, abandon you or treat you cruelly at the worst possible time. And some of the people you least expect to show up, somehow step up and support you in ways you never imagined. I experienced it and I hear it over and over again in my support groups. It's a painful, bittersweet process that changes your perspective. Fingers crossed I am a better judge of character now.

As a cancer survivor myself I find nothing in common with someone who lives the life of royalty. She didn’t have the same life experience that most of us have. No worries about the expenses involved or finding the right specialist. No worries about keeping house, shopping for necessities or paying bills. The children have a nanny to help and someone is always available to drive to the doctor or treatment center. 

I sympathize with anyone who had or has cancer. A story about how someone who lives a privileged life is dealing with an unknown cancer is a waste of time.

But I also know how deeply painful abandonment is (from close friends), and that even when there is reconciliation when the child grows up, that small things in everyday life can trigger pain, anger, and coldness. I don’t doubt the good memories, and I also recognize that the author showed more grace and goodwill than the vast majority of the population, but something about the telling of this story just feels a little  off, a little too generous to the author. I think the thing that was explained the least - that he returned to a war-torn country - may reveal a lot more about the difficulties of broken relationships, even when both sides try to fix them. comments.name: ChrisBr
comments.body: My future wife and I arrived for a vacation in England in September 1989, much of which was intended for us to indulge our mutual love of theater. On our list of shows was the Daniel Day-Lewis "Hamlet" at the National, to see an actor whom my wife, in particular, had become enamored with after seeing him in the film "My Beautiful Laundrette." When we arrived at the box office on the day of the performance to pick up our tickets, we were saddened to learn that Day-Lewis had dropped out of the production and that Hamlet was now being played by his understudy, Jeremy Northam. We still attended the performance, but suffice it to say we were thoroughly disappointed by the performance of Northam, who struck us as a supercilious Hamlet but whom I am pleased to say we have since recognized as a fine actor in his own right -- just not as Hamlet, at least under those circumstances. We wish we could have seen Ian Charleson, who took over the role of Hamlet a few weeks later.

Actors are funny: each has their own techniques to drop the mask that lies to protect us from the world and thereby expose the truth to anyone who cares to see. In Elsinore for me the mask comes off most fully in the beach scene with Derek Jarman.

comments.name: Michael Gorra

The best scene was indeed the quasi-incestuous pas de deux with Judi Dench's Gertrude. The whole thing clearly took an enormous amount out of him, and somehow I wasn't surprised to read, some weeks later, that he had walked off the stage.  You felt that he wanted to, wanted to escape an imprisoning role, a role he felt he had to play.  But then that's precisely what Hamlet wants to do as well.

comments.name: Martha Peterson
comments.body:
Does the neck really need to be strengthened or is the problem somewhere else, more central?
Somatic Education has a different perspective  readers might relate to:

When we’re worried, fearful, or sit for long hours at a desk hunched over, our brain teaches the front of our body to shorten, as if to protect ourselves. The chest collapses, the abdominals tighten, shoulders come forward and the face is pulled forward.  This full body  posture of holding is called the Startle Response. The more you respond to it in daily life, the more habituated it becomes. And this is what contributes to your neck pain. 

The key is to become aware of where you’re holding unconscious, high levels of tension that contribute to things like “tech neck,” back pain, hip pain, limited mobility  - then learn how to voluntarily release them. It’s about retraining your brain to retrain your muscles to fully release and relax. That’s what we teach in Somatic Education: improved function and awareness leads to less pain, more mobility, and more control.

It’s less about your neck and more where your brain can neither sense nor fully relax the muscles of the front that are pulling your face forward and creating neck pain. 

Check out a simple Somatic Movement called the Flower. 
Find it on the Essential Somatics or LearnSomatics Youtube channel. You’ll learn how to voluntarily contract into your pattern of tension, then slowly come out of it as if yawning. 
I’m curious to know what people experience.

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body:
Contrary to what the reporter and others in the televised report said, Krampus has traditionally absolutely nothing to do with North America’s Santa Claus and certainly not with Christmas.He accompanies St. Nikolaus (no, that is not Santa Claus ) on December 6th i.e. here in Germany as he goes from house to house (by invitation) in the evening visiting children. Nikolaus (who was a bishop in Myra) has a golden book with stories (from parents ) of good and not so good things the kids have done over the year and what they might better in the coming year. Krampus shakes a stick at the kids when the bad stuff is told. He is not a monster, doesn’t talk and has no nasty, bloody teeth.  He is not there to “terrify“ children. Nikolaus gives the kids a sack traditionally filled with fruit, nuts sweets. Often family and neighbors gather in one home to welcome Nikolaus together. Children are invited to sing or recite a traditional poem they have learned. On Christmas Eve (Dec. 24th) the Christ child comes and secretly leaves presents - different story.
That Krampus in the parade was dressed in red is ridiculous. He wears ruddy clothes/rags and St. Nikolaus wears a red cloak which, according to legend he tore and shared with a beggar who was freezing. Perhaps before one randomly adopts culture from another country one should understand it, so as not to misrepresent it. My meager opinion. And yes, I do think Santa is great and has his rightful place in the world. Reindeer and all! 🤗

My obituary partner and I were both 19, and what you have done when you're 19?  It was harder than you would think and both our obituaries sounded so trite...  She went into some aspect of journalism and I became an accountant.   But I keep track of the deaths of my high school classmates (high school was a long time ago--let's just say Nixon was still president) and I notify our classmates.  Many people don't publish obituaries through funeral homes, or they moved away, or their families don't know who to tell, or I get notified by people who knew them well but have no authority to publish an obituary.  Or I hear from people who "thought they heard".  The lack of a published obituary means very little. So I hold onto them till I find a second confirmation.  I have my ways.  I held onto to one for seven years.  Finally, I tracked down the classmate's sister and asked her.   He's alive.  The person who told me--our class president--was so sure... that good old Bob had passed.   My word of choice is "died".  I don't generally state the cause of death.

comments.name: bill steigerwald
comments.body: Obits were often considered the purgatory or the gulag of the  newspaper biz. It's where interns and washed up hacks were stationed. It was not a place for good writing.  At the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, the deaths of the un-famous were often reduced to having their names, ages and places of death plugged into brisk templates that had spaces to fill in the funeral parlor and places of interment . At the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette in the 1990s the editor, John Craig, was smart enough to realize the power of the obit. He instituted a policy that all writers and reporters, even the hotshots, had to spend a week doing local obituaries that were well written and of appropriate length  -- nice little feature stories on deadline, as it were.  It was a genius move -- not only did it give value to readers and honor to the departed, it was a smart PR move. Obits of local grocers, doctors  and political hacks  were read by their loved ones and sometimes hundreds of their friends. Writing an obit took a few hours -- calls to the funeral home and a call or two to get quotes and anecdotes from a relative or friend of the dead. Once I got a call from the wife of my obit subject. I once looked at what it would take my company to upgrade our old Java servers and the answer was on the order of years. Now there is ai coding and new vulnerabilities so companies are going to try to fix those things they used to call “tech debt”. Many of these tasks are borderline impossible and likely inadvisable. But the newly exposed exploits mean it’s a rock and hard place decision for engineering teams.

Couple this with features being released at ever increasing rate, without a comparable change in approach or infrastructure, and this will be the new normal for a year or two, or possibly the rest of the life of the internet as we know it. Today’s network and router technology is not hugely different than what it was 30 years ago.

Welcome to the new normal.

Software products are shipped with known bugs.  Partly due to time pressures, but partly due to whenever you modify complex code to fix one bug, you might introduce another.  So unless the severity is high or someone will likely encounter it, you ship.

With AI, all of a sudden released software has a lot more “known” bugs, which are suddenly potentially known to bad actors.  Some of these bugs are too severe to ignore.   If really severe, you take your system down until you can patch it.  Either way, you rush through an emergency patch.  Which may require a system reboot at release (a short interruption), but otherwise fine.   But like any modification, especially one done quickly, it might introduce new bugs.  Some of which might result in more shutdowns.  And the cycle continues.

Collodi’s involvement in the Risorgimento does not preclude a Christian reading of Pinocchio, since political opposition to ecclesiastical authority is not equivalent to a rejection of Christian theology, and the novel’s themes of sin, repentance, grace, and redemption remain deeply rooted in the Christian moral tradition. Pinocchio’s rebellion against his creator, Geppetto, echoes humanity’s rebellion against God through the misuse of free will. His pursuit of unrestricted freedom ultimately enslaves him, most explicitly through his transformation into a donkey, illustrating the Christian understanding of sin as bondage. Yet the Blue Fairy repeatedly extends undeserved mercy, embodying divine grace and forgiveness, while his escape from the Dogfish recalls the biblical account of Jonah and symbolizes spiritual rebirth. Pinocchio becomes truly human not through the satisfaction of his desires, but through repentance, self-denial and sacrificial love—a transformation profoundly consonant with the Christian understanding of redemption.

An interesting aside is how Elena Ferrante uses Pinocchio via "The BLue Fairy"as a touchstone in her epic "My Brilliant Friend."

With the more contemporary Walt Disney and Pixar films of my childhood, I glanced over Pinocchio as another tale, like Peter Pan (which I was more sympathetic towards): a whimsical child’s night dream, only to wake up and wish to discover something like it the next night. Such tales, however special they remind us of the simpler times, are an ode to the veneer of rot that lingers below the surface, and the purity that lingers within it, if you can find it.

Almost every time there is a problem, something gets mishandled: eg. Lost requisitions, wrong parts ordered or delivered, repairs that don’t address the problem. At this point he hesitates to use his power chair because the steering mechanism oversteers and is hard to control in a small space. He’s told it seems fine- it isn’t. I’ve driven it and I’ve been driving/ moving his wheelchairs for 35 years. His GF, who is severely affected, has had to use a “ backup” chair w resultant terrible pain since she’s had to wait for someone to repair her own specially fitted power chair. 
I’m simultaneously glad to see you address this and horrified to realize that the change in responsiveness of the once local company is profit driven private equity.

Another said that when her wheelchair stopped being able help her stand and stretch, weeks of constant nerve pain left her unable to work and hardly able to sleep.

If you or someone you know has dealt with wheelchair repair delays, I’d like to hear your story.

I read Ishi 55 years ago in undergraduate school at the recommendation of an anthropology professor. It is a heartbreaking story. Ishi emerges badly  burned from a California wildfire , speaking only his indigenous language and evidently as the last living member of his tribe. He is traumatized and spends the rest of his days on exhibit in a California museum making stone tools for a daily audience, in a glassed in exhibit "cage" as I recall.Our professor invited us quietly to just sit with it as we might say these days.
I'm not indigenous but my children have indigenous blood and don't have to live in a cage to survive.
The book sounds powerful and distressing.There is a lot of reckoning on offer and I commend the author and think the review is also excellent. I visited Yosemite and saw that rockface. People do navigate it capably and I suppose some of them begin very young. What a horrible memory though to have one's own father make such a careless error with one's life.

comments.body:
There are quite a few phrases that only my family use- too many to list here, if I’m honest, and many of them I don’t pick up on, as I’m so used to hearing them.

The most obvious ones are the Yiddish and Hebrew integrations. I come from a Jewish family, and while neither language is fluently spoken within my house, it seeps through the cracks as slang. The two words/phrases most commonly used are ‘Meshuga’ (Yiddish, meaning crazy) and ‘Ein ba aya’ (Hebrew, no problem), as both are frequently necessary within my house!

Beyond that, in my house, ceiling lights are called owls (Yes, like the animal). This comes from an instance during a holiday lights tour at the Morton Arboretum, where my mother mistook a partially obscured chandelier-like display for an owl. "But Calyx," you say, "Those things look nothing alike!" I know, dear reader. I don’t know how she managed it either.
